title: Schemes for School, Skills and Work

level-1.title: Help with school things
summary: School costs money. Books, uniforms, bus fare and hostel fees all cost money.
The government gives money to Deaf students to help pay for these things.
This money is called a scholarship. It is not a loan. You never pay it back.
You do not have to be top of the class. It is because you are Deaf, not because of marks.
A trusted adult applies for it with you, using your UDID card.

questions.prompt: Your cousin took a bank loan for a laptop and now repays some money every month. You received a scholarship for your school books. What is the key difference in what happens next?

image.alt: A loan repayment beside a scholarship for books

options.label: Your cousin must keep repaying the loan; you never have to repay the scholarship
Both of you must repay eventually
Neither of you ever has to repay anything

questions.hint: Only one of the two - a loan or a scholarship - is ever paid back.

questions.prompt: A classmate says 'you only got the scholarship because you're the top student.' Based on the lesson, is this true?

image.alt: A classmate comparing exam marks to a scholarship letter

options.label: No - it is because of being Deaf, not because of exam marks
Yes, only top students ever qualify
It depends on which subject you are best at

questions.hint: The lesson is specific about what qualifies a student, and it is not about being top of the class.

questions.prompt: A trusted adult is helping you apply for the school scholarship, but they cannot find your ID card anywhere. Which specific card do they need to find first?

image.alt: An adult searching for a specific identity card

options.label: The UDID card
A library card
A birthday card

questions.hint: It is the same card the previous lesson was entirely about.

level-2.title: Scholarships, training and a job
summary: Pre-Matric scholarships cover Classes IX and X. Post-Matric covers Class XI upward - school, diploma, degree and postgraduate study.
They can pay tuition, hostel and book costs, and add a disability allowance on top.
They usually need 40% disability, a valid UDID and a family income under a set limit.
After school there is more. PM-DAKSH gives free vocational training and helps with placement. A free coaching scheme pays for exam coaching - UPSC, SSC, banking, state exams.
For research there is a National Fellowship covering M.Phil. and Ph.D. study, with a monthly amount.
In government jobs, 4% of posts are reserved for disabled candidates, and 1% of that is held for deaf and hard-of-hearing people alone. There is also age relaxation and lower exam fees.
Every one of these needs an application, a deadline and papers. Missing the deadline is the commonest way this money is lost.

questions.prompt: A student has just finished Class X and is about to start Class XI. Which scholarship category do they now move into?

image.alt: A student moving from Class X into Class XI

options.label: Post-Matric - Class XI is past the 'Matric' dividing line
They stay in Pre-Matric until Class XII
Neither applies once you pass Class X

questions.hint: The dividing line is exactly between Class X and Class XI.

questions.prompt: A student has a 45% disability and a valid UDID card, but their family's income is above the scheme's set limit. Can they receive the Post-Matric scholarship?

image.alt: A qualifying disability percentage beside an income limit that is exceeded

options.label: Not under the standard rules - all conditions, including income, usually need to be met
Yes, disability percentage alone is enough
Yes, since they have a UDID card

questions.hint: The lesson lists three separate conditions, not just one or two.

questions.prompt: Three students want different things: one wants vocational job training, one wants coaching for a banking exam, and one wants funding for a PhD. Which scheme matches each?

image.alt: Three students with three different goals

options.label: PM-DAKSH for training, Free Coaching for the exam, National Fellowship for the PhD
All three should apply to PM-DAKSH
Free Coaching covers all three needs

questions.hint: Each of the three schemes named in the lesson has one specific purpose.

level-3.title: Turning entitlements into income
summary: Put together, these schemes are a route: study paid for, skills trained, a reserved share of jobs, and tax relief once you earn.
Scholarship and fellowship money is paid into a bank account in your own name - which is why the account came first in this course.
NHFDC lends at concessional rates for study or for starting your own business, for people who want to work for themselves rather than be hired.
States add their own: marriage assistance, self-employment loans, free laptops, housing support, free bus travel. These vary enormously, so check your own state rather than assuming.
Scholarship money is income you did not have to earn. Treated as spending money it disappears; put into savings or a SIP it becomes the start of something.
That is where this whole course meets: budget it, bank it, grow it, and know what you are owed.
Amounts, income limits and deadlines change every year. Verify on the official portal before relying on any figure taught here.

questions.prompt: A scholarship officer asks for your bank account details, but you only have access to a joint account held with a relative. Why might this specifically be a problem, based on this whole course?

image.alt: A joint account shared with a relative, receiving a scholarship

options.label: Money you are owed is meant to be paid into an account you fully control, not one you share - the same point made about bank accounts and funds
It is not a problem at all, joint accounts work identically
It is only a problem if the relative is unemployed

questions.hint: This connects directly to why the course insisted on your OWN account, several lessons ago.

questions.prompt: A student wants to start a small tailoring business rather than continue studying. A friend suggests a Post-Matric scholarship. Is this the right scheme for their goal?

image.alt: A tailoring business being set up, beside a scholarship form

options.label: No - a scholarship is for study; NHFDC's concessional loan is designed for self-employment like this
Yes, scholarships also fund businesses
Neither scheme applies to starting a business

questions.hint: One of the two schemes is specifically about study costs, and the other is about work and self-employment.

questions.prompt: You receive a ₹6000 scholarship. Option A: spend all of it now. Option B: put ₹4000 into savings or a SIP and spend ₹2000. Which option leaves you with something a year from now, and why?

image.alt: Two paths for the same scholarship money, one year later

options.label: Option B - money that is saved or invested can still exist and possibly grow a year later; fully spent money is gone
Option A - spending it all now means you enjoyed it fully
Both options leave you with exactly the same amount a year later

questions.hint: The lesson's very last idea is about what happens to money depending on whether it is spent or kept.
